nameStory: The flat periwinkle gets its name from its distinctly flattened shell shape, which sets it apart from its more dome-shaped cousins. The word "periwinkle" comes from the Old English "pinewincle," meaning "little spiral shell," though this species shows less of that classic spiral than other periwinkles.
description: The flat periwinkle is a small sea snail that clings to seaweed and rocks along New England's rocky shores. Its shell is notably flattened and smooth, typically ranging from yellow to orange to brown in color. These tiny marine snails are much smaller than the common periwinkles you might find in tide pools, rarely exceeding half an inch across. They're actually marine gastropods, which means they're related to garden snails but have adapted to life in the salty intertidal zone.

idTips.label: Flattened shell shape
idTips.description: The shell feels distinctly pressed down and low-profile when you run your finger over it, much flatter than other periwinkles which feel more like little domes

idTips.label: Smooth shell texture
idTips.description: The shell surface is glossy and smooth to the touch, lacking the ridges or rough texture of other periwinkle species

idTips.label: Variable coloration
idTips.description: Colors range from bright yellow and orange to dark brown, often matching the color of the seaweed they live on

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically less than half an inch across, feeling like a small button between your fingers

idTips.label: Seaweed habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found crawling on bladder wrack and other brown seaweeds rather than directly on rocks

habitat: Flat periwinkles live in the intertidal zone along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly where brown seaweeds like bladder wrack and knotted wrack grow abundantly. You'll find them clinging to these seaweeds in the mid to upper tide zones, from Maine's granite shores down to the rocky headlands of Massachusetts and Rhode Island. They prefer areas with good water circulation and avoid muddy or sandy beaches.

seasonality.spring: Active feeding and movement becomes more noticeable as water temperatures warm. This is when you're most likely to spot them crawling on fresh seaweed growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with easiest observation during low tides. Their varied colors are most vibrant and they're actively grazing on seaweed surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek more sheltered positions among seaweed holdfasts and rock crevices as storms increase.
seasonality.winter: Less active and harder to spot, often tucked deep into seaweed clumps or rock crevices. Look for them during calm, low tide periods on warmer winter days.

funFact: Flat periwinkles are master color-matchers that can actually change their shell color over time to perfectly blend with their seaweed homes - yellow ones live on yellow bladder wrack, brown ones on brown rockweed, creating nearly perfect camouflage that would make a chameleon jealous!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with young common periwinkles, but flat periwinkles have that distinctive pressed-down, flattened look while common periwinkles are always more dome-shaped. Remember: "flat periwinkle, flat shell" - if it looks like someone gently squished it from above, you've found the right species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "flat" periwinkles, they're still three-dimensional snails - the name refers to their shell being flatter than other periwinkles, not actually pancake-flat. Many beachgoers overlook them entirely because they blend so well with seaweed and are much smaller than the common periwinkles that dominate tide pool attention.
compareHints: Compared to common periwinkles, flat periwinkles are much smaller, flatter, and live primarily on seaweed rather than rocks. Rough periwinkles are closer in size but have distinctly ridged, textured shells and prefer higher, drier areas of the shore. Flat periwinkles are the only local periwinkle species with that characteristic squished-down appearance and smooth, glossy shell surface.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common periwinkles are larger and darker than their flat periwinkle cousins, which are yellow, orange, or brown and have a more flattened, less pointed shell.
Unlike the common periwinkle which has a smooth shell, the rough periwinkle's distinctly bumpy texture sets it apart immediately.
